content: The most widely accepted definition today is the international avoirdupois pound, which is precisely equal to 453.59237 grams. The term pound originates from the Latin word pendere, meaning to weigh, while the Latin word libra, meaning scales or balances, also referred to a Roman unit of mass similar to the pound. This is the source of the abbreviation lb for the pound. Historically, the pound has been defined differently across various regions, time periods, and applications, leading to standards of mass or weight that are broadly similar but not identical. English Pounds In England, several definitions of the pound have been used, including the avoirdupois pound, as well as the now-obsolete Troy, Tower, Merchant's, and London pounds. Historically, there was a connection between the pound as a unit of mass and the pound as a unit of currency. For instance, the pound sterling was originally equivalent to the value of a Tower pound of silver. In 1528, the standard shifted to the Troy pound. Avoirdupois Pound The avoirdupois pound was introduced by London merchants in 1303. During the reign of Henry VIII, it was redefined as 7,000 troy grains. The grain became a fundamental part of the avoirdupois system.453592338 kilograms. This older value is sometimes referred to as the imperial pound, though this terminology is now obsolete. In the United States, the avoirdupois pound has been officially defined in terms of the kilogram since 1893. Initially, the conversion was set at 2.20462 pounds per kilogram, later refined to 2.20462234 pounds per kilogram in 1894. This adjustment was based on the British pound. The current international pound, established in 1958, differs from the 1894 U.S. pound by about one part in 10 million. The international avoirdupois pound is now defined as exactly 453.59237 grams. The avoirdupois pound is subdivided into 16 avoirdupois ounces or 7,000 grains. The conversion factor between the kilogram and the international pound was chosen to be divisible by 7, making an international grain exactly 64.79891 milligrams. Troy Pound The troy pound derives its name from the French market town of Troyes, where English merchants traded as early as the time of Charlemagne. The troy weight system was historically used in England by apothecaries and jewelers. A troy pound consists of 12 troy ounces or 5,760 grains. Today, the troy pound is equivalent to 373.241721 grams. Although the troy pound is no longer in general use, the troy ounce remains the standard for measuring precious metals like gold, silver, and platinum, as well as some gemstones. The use of the troy pound was abolished in the United Kingdom on January 6, 1879. However, in contexts involving precious metals, references to pounds often imply troy pounds, even if not explicitly stated. Merchant's Pound The merchant's pound, also known as the mercantile pound or libra mercantoria, was equivalent to 9,600 wheat grains (15 Tower ounces or 6,750 grains). It was used in England until the 14th century for most goods, excluding money, spices, and electuaries. London Pound The London pound was equivalent to 7,200 troy grains (16 Tower ounces or 15 troy ounces). Roman Libra The libra, a Roman unit of mass, was approximately 327 grams and was divided into 12 unciae (ounces). The abbreviation lb for the pound originates from the libra. French Livre In France, various pounds, known as livres, were used during the Middle Ages. The livre esterlin, used between the late 9th and mid-14th centuries, was approximately 367 grams. The livre poids de marc, or livre de Paris, introduced in the 1350s, was about 489.5 grams. The livre métrique, introduced in 1800, was defined as equal to one kilogram but was abolished in 1812. The livre usuelle, set at 500 grams, was introduced in 1812 but abolished in 1840. Russian Funt The Russian funt, an obsolete unit of mass, was equivalent to 409.5124 grams. Jersey Pound The Jersey pound, used on the island of Jersey from the 14th to the 19th century, was approximately 7,561 grains. It may have been derived from the French livre poids de marc. Trone Pound The trone pound, an obsolete Scottish unit of mass, ranged between 21 and 28 avoirdupois ounces. Metric Pounds In many countries, the introduction of the metric system led to the pound being informally redefined as half a kilogram (500 grams). For example, in the Netherlands, the pond was officially redefined as one kilogram but is now commonly used to refer to 500 grams. Similarly, in Germany, the term Pfund refers to 500 grams. Older definitions of the pound, such as those in Spain, Portugal, and Latin America (approximately 459–460 grams), and Norway (498.1 grams), have been replaced. Use in Commerce In the United States, the pound is defined in commerce as the avoirdupois pound, often referred to as Net Weight. Federal regulations, such as those outlined in NIST Handbook 130, govern the use of mass and weight in trade.
